review.decision_difference: Choose B to freeze expansion and first validate that a narrow founder segment repeatedly obtains useful, evidence-backed shortlists with measurable advantage over manual search; test approval-first outreach only after that foundation passes. Choosing A would instead validate shortlist and drafting together, producing stronger end-to-end evidence but a less diagnostic initial sequencing decision.
review.rationale: B more cleanly isolates the discovery-and-qualification mechanism before outreach introduces offer quality, sender reputation, and platform reliability as confounders. Its bounded cohort, manual-search comparison, predefined thresholds, downstream-use measurement, and repeat-task window make rejection more credible and directly govern whether to continue, pivot, stop, or sequence outreach next. A tests a valuable end-to-end loop, but its broader scope makes failure attribution less precise and its benchmark proposal is less explicit about comparative value and bounded thresholds.

review.decision_difference: Choose A to first establish whether existing rules create retained value at the merge boundary; pursue B's multi-repository shared authority only after that signal survives.
review.rationale: A isolates workflow placement as the next causal adoption mechanism and uses a bounded single-repository probe with explicit thresholds for continuing, pivoting, or stopping. B tests a consequential shared-authority opportunity, but simultaneously varies repository count, central ownership, remote policy delivery, and required enforcement, making negative results harder to diagnose.

review.decision_difference: Choose B to test whether the existing forkable routing component is independently useful behind adopter-owned infrastructure before implementing native production controls. Choose A only if the immediate decision is already narrowed to whether a minimally authenticated production-like gateway can operate safely.
review.rationale: B more cleanly tests the required boundary using reproducibility, failure semantics, independent evaluation, and comparison with established alternatives. It can reveal whether the gateway has distinct value as a routing component or whether adopters actually require native operational controls. A strongly tests safety invariants, but it begins by adding authentication and deadlines, partially committing to the production-control-layer boundary before establishing that this boundary is needed; its adopter-interest criterion is also less bounded by public repository evidence.
